subject: Chemistry
topic: Acids, bases and pH — mixed tiers
description: Definitions, indicators, common laboratory acids/bases, neutralisation, real-world examples

questions.stem: According to the Arrhenius theory, an ACID is a substance that:

options.option_text: Releases H⁺ (hydrogen ion / proton) in aqueous solution

questions.explanation: Arrhenius (1884) — Acid releases H⁺; Base releases OH⁻ in water. HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻; NaOH → Na⁺ + OH⁻. Brønsted-Lowry (1923) generalised: acid = proton donor, base = proton acceptor (works for non-aqueous). Lewis theory (1923) — most general: acid = electron-pair acceptor, base = electron-pair donor. Different theories explain different reactions but Arrhenius is the school-textbook level.

questions.explanation: pH = −log₁₀[H⁺]. Theoretical scale 0-14 at room temperature (in water). pH 0 = strong acid (1 M HCl); pH 14 = strong base (1 M NaOH); pH 7 = neutral pure water. Each 1 unit = 10× change in [H⁺]. Acidic: pH 0-6 (lemon ~2, vinegar ~2.5, tomato ~4.5, coffee ~5). Neutral: pH 7. Basic: pH 8-14 (baking soda ~9, ammonia ~11, bleach ~12). Strong acids (concentrated battery acid) can go below 0; very alkaline solutions can go above 14.

questions.explanation: Litmus — natural dye from lichen Roccella tinctoria. BLUE litmus → RED in acid. RED litmus → BLUE in base. Stays the same in neutral. Two-paper test confirms acidity / basicity. Other indicators: PHENOLPHTHALEIN — colourless in acid/neutral, PINK in base (transition pH 8.3-10). METHYL ORANGE — red in acid, yellow above pH 4.4 (transition 3.1-4.4). UNIVERSAL INDICATOR — multi-colour spectrum showing pH numerical estimate. pH meter (electronic) is most precise.

questions.stem: When an acid reacts with a base to form salt + water, the reaction is called:
questions.explanation: Neutralisation: HA + BOH → BA + H₂O (acid + base → salt + water). Standard enthalpy of neutralisation ≈ −57.3 kJ/mol for any strong-acid + strong-base reaction (since the reaction is essentially H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O). Real-world examples: antacids neutralising stomach acid (Mg(OH)₂ in milk of magnesia, NaHCO₃ in baking soda); using lime to neutralise acidic soil; toothpaste (slight base) neutralising acidic plaque. Strong acid + weak base (e.g., HCl + NH₄OH) gives slightly acidic salt; strong base + weak acid → slightly basic salt.

questions.stem: Among the following, the STRONGEST acid in aqueous solution is:

options.option_text: Hydrochloric acid (HCl) — fully dissociates in water

questions.explanation: Strong acids (~100% dissociation in water) — HCl, HBr, HI, H₂SO₄ (1st step), HNO₃, HClO₄. Weak acids partial — CH₃COOH (vinegar, Ka ~1.8×10⁻⁵, pKa 4.76), H₂CO₃ (very weak, pKa1 6.35), citric (~3.13), lactic, oxalic. Among given options, HCl is strongest. 'Stomach acid' is dilute HCl, pH ~1.5-2. 'Aqua regia' = 3:1 HCl:HNO₃ — dissolves gold/platinum.

questions.explanation: Baking soda = NaHCO₃ (sodium bicarbonate). Mildly basic (pH ~8.3 in solution). On heating: 2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂ (releases CO₂ → bread/cake rises). Also a mild antacid. Used in fire extinguishers (releases CO₂ smothering flames). 'Washing soda' is sodium CARBONATE — Na₂CO₃·10H₂O — strongly basic, removes hard-water Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ ions. NaCl = common salt. NaOH = caustic soda — very strong base, used in soap-making (saponification).

questions.stem: If a solution has [H⁺] = 10⁻⁵ M, its pH is:
questions.explanation: pH = −log₁₀[H⁺] = −log(10⁻⁵) = 5. Slightly acidic. To find pOH: pH + pOH = 14 (at 25 °C) → pOH = 9. [OH⁻] = 10⁻⁹ M. Quick conversion table: [H⁺] 10⁻¹ → pH 1; 10⁻⁷ → pH 7 (neutral); 10⁻¹³ → pH 13. Each integer step in pH means a 10× change in [H⁺]. pH 4 vs pH 6 → 100× more acidic.
